newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Green Cross sees merger pact by October.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Green Cross sees merger pact by October.

text.p: Scandal-tainted Japanese drug maker Green Cross Corp says it hopes to sign a formal merger agreement with Yoshitomi Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd by October.
"It's possible we will sign the merger agreement in October or even little bit earlier than that," Green Cross managing director Kazumasa Yokoyama told Reuters in a recent interview.

Green Cross has been at the centre of a scandal concerning the sale of HIV-tainted blood products. The scandal caused a sharp fall in its sales and last October three of its former presidents were indicted on charges of professional negligence.
In February, the two Osaka-based drug companies announced that Yoshitomi would take over Green Cross on October 1. However, they said in May that the merger was postponed until April 1, 1998.
Yokoyama said talks on unifying sales agents and harmonising business operations were moving forward.
He also said Green Cross hoped to apply to the Health Ministry in September for approval to make a new blood product, recombinant-human serum albumin.
The company had hoped to apply for the government approval last year, but clinical testing of the product, which is used to treat excess bleeding, was delayed due to the scandal.
The company now aims to launch the product in 2000.
Yokoyama said Green Cross was considering closing down one of its Osaka factories as part of efforts to restructure ahead of the merger.
He said the number of Green Cross employees had declined by about 150 over the last year from about 2,400 as it stopped hiring new recruits.

Nevertheless, he said: "In order to survive, we have to develop breakthrough medicines in the areas of circulatory and immune systems. So we don't plan to cut staff in research and development even after the merger."
He said Green Cross blood products and Yoshitomi's drugs to treat nerve disorders would likely be the two main pillers of the merged company.
He said that the boycott of Green Cross products prompted by public outrage at the scandal was subsiding.

However, he said the company's total sales in the current business year to March 1998 were likely to improve by only about 10 percent from the previous year, affected by the government's cut in drug reimbursement rates under the National Health Insurance system.
Yokoyama said a total of 1,200 patients infected with the HIV virus by Green Cross blood products had so far filed lawsuits against the company.
The company expects the compensation payments it will have to pay to total about 24 billion yen.
